answers.text: Same idea as before — three lines every time, same order: delivery date, item and quantity, then any change from the original order. Keep the date format and item name consistent every time so the three lines don't drift between runs.

The memo needs the same four lines every time, same order — date, amount, category, submitter — with the total worked out as the sum of that week's amounts, shown to two decimals. If two lines look like the same claim repeated, I'd flag it rather than add both in without asking.

This one doesn't hold together, so it shouldn't go out as drafted. It's not the price — 100 times 48.50 is exactly 4,850, that's correct — the problem is the dates: the 19th is five days after the 14th, not three, and 'three days out from today' would put today around the 16th, which doesn't square with 'following our call on the 14th'. Two of those can't both be true. Before sending, I'd check the actual confirmed delivery date and today's date against the dispatch system rather than just re-reading the email.

62 versus 54 does work out to about a 15% rise, so that part's fine. The first real problem is the on-time rate — 3 late out of 62 is close to 95%, not 97% as stated. Second, stock is said to have 'held steady' at 340 (170 at each depot) — the two depot figures add up fine on their own, but with deliveries up 15% that week, stock staying exactly flat needs an explanation the report doesn't give. Before this goes up, I'd check both the late-delivery count and the stock figures against the depot records directly, not just recheck the numbers already in the report.

I'd sign off Output 2, the one showing 612,000 and 25,100, not just the 4.1%. Output 1 only gives the percentage — no sales figure, no returns figure, nothing to check it against. 4.1% might well be right, but there's no way to know that without going and running the numbers myself.

I'd send Reply 2 without more checking — it's got the order number and the credit reference in it. Reply 1 just says 'this was entirely our error' with nothing behind that to check. That doesn't make Reply 1 wrong necessarily — it might be fine too, once someone's actually confirmed we caused the delay.

1. Delivery address — no, that identifies a specific customer. 2. Sales total, aggregate — yes, no names in it. 3. Next quarter's pricing — no, not released yet. 4. Spec sheet — yes, already public on our site, no reason to hold it back. 5. Colleague's mobile — no, that's personal, not mine to share.

Pricing and volume discounts I'd hold back — that's commercial detail, not something to paste into a tool we haven't cleared. The confidentiality clause is the same kind of problem, since it names both companies directly.
I'd have the weekly totals cross-checked against the depot system directly rather than just read over, and that check sits before the report goes to the manager on Friday, not after.

Step 1 is the one that worries me — if the AI misreads the order email, the wrong numbers carry through the rest of the process. Step 4, the automatic send, is where it actually needs a proper look before anything goes out, since that's the point nothing can be pulled back.
